paras.text: MIOSHA Construction Safety, Audio Lecture

MIOSHA safety is worth about ten of the one hundred ten trade questions on your exam, and it is the easiest ten on the test. Here is why. Safety questions are number questions. Heights, depths, hours, dollars. There is almost no judgment in them.

But there is a catch, and it is the reason people lose these easy points. Several of these numbers come in pairs that look interchangeable and are not. Six and ten. Four and five. Twenty and ten. Eight and twenty four. The exam writes its wrong answers by handing you the other number in the pair.
So the way I am going to teach this is by the pairs. Learn them as pairs and the traps disappear.
Idea one. Who MIOSHA is, and the two agency traps.

MIOSHA is the Michigan Occupational Safety and Health Administration, created by the MIOSHA Act, Act one fifty four of nineteen seventy four. Michigan runs its own state plan, which by federal law has to be at least as effective as federal OSHA.

Now the discriminator the exam likes. MIOSHA covers public sector employees, meaning state, county, and city workers. Federal OSHA does not. So if a question asks who MIOSHA protects that federal OSHA does not, the answer is public employees.

And the second trap, who runs it. The Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity, L E O. Not LARA. It moved from LARA to L E O by executive order in twenty nineteen. On construction sites the enforcement arm is the Construction Safety and Health Division.

You have now met L E O twice, because it also runs workers compensation. LARA licenses you. L E O regulates how you work and what happens when somebody gets hurt. If an answer choice says LARA administers MIOSHA, that is the trap.

Then the rule that catches everything the specific standards miss, the General Duty Clause. Every employer must furnish a workplace free from recognized hazards that are causing or likely to cause death or serious physical harm. That is M C L four oh eight point ten eleven.

The key to using it is knowing when it applies. It applies when no specific standard covers the hazard. It is the catch all, which is why an unusual hazard with no rule of its own still gets you cited.
And under the construction general rules, every construction employer must have an accident prevention program. Not optional, and not waived because you run a small crew.
Question. Who administers MIOSHA, and who does MIOSHA cover that federal OSHA does not.
The Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity, L E O, not LARA. And public sector employees.
Idea two. The first pair, six and ten. This is the most tested trap in the domain.
Fall protection is Part forty five, and the general trigger is six feet. If a work area is six feet or more above a lower level, workers need fall protection.
Three conventional systems. Guardrails. Safety nets. Or a personal fall arrest system, meaning harness, lanyard, and anchorage.

The guardrail numbers. A top rail sits at forty two inches, plus or minus three, and it has to take a two hundred pound force. In a personal fall arrest system, maximum free fall is six feet, and the rig cannot let the worker hit a lower level. The anchorage must hold five thousand pounds per worker.

And on a residential roof, where conventional systems are truly infeasible at a particular spot, the fallback is a written, site specific fall protection plan. Written. Not a decision you make in your head that morning.
Now the other half of the pair. Scaffolds are Part twelve, and a guardrail on the open side of a scaffold platform is required at ten feet. Not six.
So read the question for the word scaffold. If it says scaffold, the answer is ten. If it says leading edge, floor opening, or just general fall protection, the answer is six.
Six for general fall protection. Ten for a scaffold guardrail. Say it back to yourself right now, because this single pair is probably worth a point on your exam.

While we are on scaffolds, the rest of Part twelve. A scaffold must support four times its maximum intended load. Planking is scaffold grade two by ten. Access must be a ladder, stair, or ramp, and climbing the cross braces is always a violation, no exceptions. Suspension type scaffolds, like a boatswain's chair or a ladder jack, require a personal fall arrest system, and a two point suspension scaffold requires both a harness system and a guardrail.
Question. A worker is on a scaffold platform eight feet up with no guardrail. Violation, yes or no. Then the same worker at eight feet on a leading edge with no protection.
On the scaffold, no violation for the missing guardrail, because the scaffold guardrail trigger is ten feet. On the leading edge, yes, a violation, because general fall protection triggers at six.
Idea three. Ladders, and the second pair, twenty and ten.
Ladders are Part eleven, and there are four things to know.
The angle is four to one. For every four feet of height, the base sits one foot out from the wall.
The extension is three feet. Side rails must extend at least three feet above the upper landing, so you have something to hold while you step off.

Put those together on a real house. A ladder to a sixteen foot eave needs to reach about nineteen feet, and the base sits about four feet out. Sixteen divided by four is four feet of base, and sixteen plus three is the nineteen.
Third, secure it. Safety feet, or tie it, block it, or otherwise fix it in place.
Fourth, never stand on the top three feet.

Now the pair. A portable ladder near power transmission or distribution lines needs twenty feet of clearance. Twenty. That is different from the ten foot clearance for equipment near lines up to fifty kilovolts.
Ladders twenty, equipment ten. It feels backwards, since the equipment is the bigger thing, and that is exactly why they test it.
Idea four. Excavations, and the third pair, four and five.
Excavation is Part nine, and this is the densest set of numbers in the chapter, so slow down with me.

A trench or excavation more than five feet deep requires a protective system. Sloping, shoring, or a trench shield. Below five feet you still need protection if the ground shows signs of hazardous movement.

Egress is a different rule with a different number. At four feet deep, forty eight inches, workers need a ladder. That ladder must extend three feet above the top of the trench and must be within twenty five feet of lateral travel of every worker in the trench.
So say it as a pair. Four feet means a ladder. Five feet means a protective system. The exam will offer you five for the ladder and four for the shoring, and both are wrong.

Two more excavation numbers. Spoil piles and equipment stay at least two feet back from the edge. And a competent person, meaning somebody who can spot hazards and has the authority to fix them, must inspect the excavation on an ongoing basis and again after every rainstorm.
Question. Trench is four and a half feet deep. What do you need, and what do you not need.

You need a ladder for egress, because that triggers at four feet, extending three feet above the top and within twenty five feet of every worker. You do not automatically need a protective system, because that triggers over five feet, unless the ground is showing signs of hazardous movement.
Idea five. Soil types, weakest to flattest.
The exam tests the federal three letter system, and there is one idea underneath all of it. The weaker the soil, the flatter you have to lay the slope back.
Type A is the most stable. Clay, silty clay. Maximum slope three quarters horizontal to one vertical, which is fifty three degrees, the steepest allowed.
Type B is the middle. Silt, angular gravel, and any previously disturbed soil. Slope one to one, forty five degrees.
Type C is the weakest. Sand, gravel, anything submerged or seeping water. Slope one and a half horizontal to one vertical, thirty four degrees, the flattest.

Two hooks to carry out of this. The weaker the soil, the flatter the slope, so the degree number goes down as the letter goes up. And previously disturbed soil can never be Type A. That second one matters on real jobs, because the ground around an existing utility has been dug before, so you are at Type B at best no matter how good the clay looks.
And before you dig at all, Michigan law says contact MISS DIG, eight one one, at least three full working days before you excavate.

Know the paint colors, they are easy points. Red is electric. Yellow is gas or oil. Orange is telecom. Blue is water. Green is sewer. White marks your proposed dig. Pink is survey. Purple is reclaimed water.
Idea six. Electrical, and the health limits.
Electrical is Part seventeen. Every one hundred twenty volt, fifteen or twenty amp receptacle that is not part of the building's permanent wiring needs G F C I protection.

There is one alternative, and know it by name. An assured equipment grounding conductor program, which is a documented testing program covering every cord set, every temporary receptacle, and every plug connected tool. So the rule is G F C I or the assured grounding program, one or the other, never neither.
And lockout tagout. Before servicing equipment, de energize it, lock it, and tag it.
Now the health numbers, which come with their own bait.
First aid. A person with a valid first aid certificate must be present at the worksite.

Silica. The permissible exposure limit is fifty micrograms per cubic meter over eight hours, and the action level is twenty five. And note the order of controls, wet cutting and vacuum collection come before respirators. Engineering controls first, protective equipment last.

Noise. In construction the limit is ninety decibels over eight hours. Now the bait, the eighty five decibel action level with hearing tests is a general industry rule, not a construction rule. They will offer you eighty five. In construction it is ninety.

Hazard communication is the right to know. Labels, safety data sheets, and training. A safety data sheet has to be on site and accessible for every hazardous chemical, no matter who brought it onto the job.
Confined spaces. Big enough to enter, limited entry and exit, not designed for occupancy. And you test the atmosphere before anybody goes in.
Idea seven. What happens when an inspector arrives, because you are the employer now.

A MIOSHA inspector who shows credentials may enter your site without delay at reasonable times. There is no advance notice, and tipping off an employer is itself an offense. You can insist on a warrant, but understand what you are buying, they will get one.
The inspection runs in a fixed order. Opening conference, walkaround, closing conference, citations. Both you and an employee representative may walk along.

Your employees have rights you should know. They can file confidential complaints. They can refuse imminently dangerous work, after asking you to fix it first. And they are protected from retaliation for doing either.
Idea eight. Penalties, and the last pair, seven and seventy.
Michigan sets its own penalty numbers, and this is where a national study book will fail you.

Serious and other than serious violations run up to seven thousand dollars each. Willful or repeat violations run up to seventy thousand, with a five thousand dollar minimum on a willful. And a willful violation that kills a worker is a felony.
If an answer choice shows the federal sixteen thousand dollar figure, it is a trap. Michigan is seven and seventy.
Then reporting, which is the pair you already met in the business chapter, so this is your second pass at it.
A fatality must be reported to MIOSHA within eight hours of learning of it. An in patient hospitalization, an amputation, or the loss of an eye must be reported within twenty four hours.
Eight for a death, twenty four for the other three, and never forty eight. Forty eight is not a MIOSHA number at all.
Recordkeeping uses three forms. The three hundred log. The three hundred A annual summary, posted from February first through April thirtieth. And the three oh one incident report.

Employers with ten or fewer employees are exempt from the routine logs. But nobody, at any size, is ever exempt from the eight hour and twenty four hour reports. Small shop, dead worker, you still call within eight hours.
Question. Two of your guys go to the hospital overnight after a fall, and you have six employees total. What do you have to do, and by when.

Report the in patient hospitalization within twenty four hours. You are exempt from keeping the routine three hundred log at six employees, but the reporting duty applies to every employer regardless of size.

One neighbor topic rides along with safety, and you have seen it twice now, so this is just reinforcement. Michigan workers compensation is required with one or more employees working thirty five or more hours a week for thirteen or more weeks, or three or more employees at any one time. And if your subcontractor has no coverage and his worker gets hurt on your job, the general contractor can be on the hook. Verify every sub's certificate.
Rapid fire recap. Say these with me, and listen for the pairs.
Fall protection, six feet. Scaffold guardrail, ten feet. Guardrail height, forty two inches, plus or minus three. Maximum free fall, six feet. Anchorage, five thousand pounds.
Ladders, four to one angle. Three feet above the landing. Ladder near power lines, twenty feet. Equipment near power lines, ten feet.
Trenches, protective system at five feet. Ladder at four feet, sticking up three feet, within twenty five feet of travel. Spoil pile, two feet back. Competent person, ongoing, and after every rain.
Soil, Type A three quarters to one at fifty three degrees. Type B one to one at forty five degrees. Type C one and a half to one at thirty four degrees. Disturbed soil is never Type A.
MISS DIG, three full working days.
Scaffolds, four times the load. Two by ten planking. Never climb the cross braces.
Electrical, G F C I on every temporary one twenty volt receptacle, or an assured grounding program.
Silica, fifty limit, twenty five action. Noise, ninety in construction.
Reporting, fatality eight hours. Hospitalization, amputation, eye, twenty four hours. Summary posted February first to April thirtieth. Ten or fewer employees, exempt from logs, never from reports.
Penalties, seven thousand serious. Seventy thousand willful or repeat, five thousand minimum.
And the agency, L E O runs MIOSHA, MIOSHA covers public employees, and the General Duty Clause fills every gap.
Ten questions, all numbers. If you only drill the four pairs, six and ten, four and five, twenty and ten, and eight and twenty four, you will still take most of these points home.
